title: A cell in a stronger bath
hook: Only water can cross the cell's edge. What happens when the bath is stronger?

knows: diffusion: things spread from crowded to less crowded
doesNotKnow: that water moves toward the more concentrated side until the two concentrations match
how to compute the final volume

misconception: Salt moves into the cell and the cell swells.
objective: The learner can explain that when only water can cross, a cell with 0.3 stuff per volume in a 0.6 bath loses water until its volume is 0.3 / 0.6 = 0.5, because the stuff inside cannot leave.

claims.text: If only water can cross a membrane, water moves toward the side with more dissolved stuff until the concentrations on the two sides match.
claims.source: Osmosis, van't Hoff ideal osmometer (Nelson, Biological Physics, 2004; Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, ch. 11).

claims.text: A toy cell with 0.3 dissolved stuff per volume, volume 1, in a bath of 0.6 where only water crosses ends at volume 0.3 / 0.6 = 0.5.
claims.source: The amount of stuff inside is fixed: 0.3 x 1 = V x 0.6, so V = 0.5. Demo.tsx computes vol(pct) = 30 / pct. Other baths shown: 0.15 gives 2.00, 0.9 gives 0.33.

claims.text: Model (stated on the stage): an ideal toy cell where only water crosses; real cells shrink less because they have walls and their own non-water bulk. Cell area is drawn proportional to volume.
claims.source: Idealised ideal-osmometer model; brief life #43. Real cell volume change is smaller because part of the volume is not water (Nelson, Biological Physics).

recall.question: Only water can cross a cell's membrane. The cell holds less dissolved stuff than the bath around it. What happens?
options: Water leaves and the cell shrinks
Water enters and the cell swells
recall.why: Water moves toward the side with more dissolved stuff, so the cell loses water until the two sides match.
